english.html: crosses, both for having taken a leg from him and made him lose a good part of his property (which that rascal du Tilh devoured and squandered), and for having presented to him on his return the horrible miseries and calamities of this prodigious deed. Wherefore to burden him further with punishment would have smacked more of the odour of some cruelty than of the integrity of justice.

Greater indeed was the difficulty with regard to the said Bertrande de Rols, for several considerations. The first, for the too great facility which she used in receiving so imprudently this cheat du Tilh for her husband, and having believed him too lightly <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>; moreover having conversed, drunk, eaten and slept with him for the space of three years under the cloak of such an error, which she approved well enough by not contradicting it <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>. Joined also (which will serve for the second reason) that during these three years she often heard murmuring, and several gave her intimations of it — nay, expressly told her that this personage was not Martin Guerre; against whom (although she had reason to believe them, or at least to doubt) she nevertheless fought vigorously, asserting the contrary — in which she seemed manifestly to disclose her fault. For just as a possessor is called a possessor in good faith until such time as he knows, or doubts, whether the parcel he has acquired belongs to another than him who delivered it to him <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>, so a woman who lies with another than her husband is excused so long as she is ignorant of it and thinks she has to do with her consort and spouse; but as soon as she comes to know the contrary, or indeed to suspect it, and nevertheless has to do with him and suffers herself to be known by him, she is inexcusable <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>: for from the moment she begins to perceive or suspect the fraud, she ought at once to separate herself from him <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup>. notes.original: l. i. P. i. D. de eo per quem fac. er. c. ſi qd lxxxvi. diſt.
notes.gloss: The canon (Gregory the Great) warns a bishop not to believe easily what he hears against a cleric. Cited again at {m}. The print's qd is quid abbreviated.
Error, cui non resistitur, approbatur — an error that is not resisted is approved: Coras's "which she approved … by not contradicting it".

notes.citation: Digest 41.1 (De adquirendo rerum dominio), l. Bonae fidei (D. 41.1.48, Paulus); Code 8.4 (Unde vi), the last law (C. 8.4.11)
notes.original: l. bona fidei. D. de acq. rer. do. l. fi. C. vnde vi.
notes.gloss: Paulus: the buyer in good faith acquires the fruits so long as he does not know the thing is another's; the possessor ceases to be in good faith when he knows or doubts.

notes.citation: Decretum, C. 34 qq. 1–2, c. Si virgo (the print has C. 33 q. 1; chapter not verified)
notes.original: c. ſi virgo. xxxiij. q. i.
notes.gloss: The woman who marries a man believing him her husband is not an adulteress until she knows; cited at annot-074 {r} and annot-077 {a}, and again below at {r}.

notes.citation: Code 5.5 (De incestis et inutilibus nuptiis), l. Qui contra, at the end (fragment not verified)
notes.original: l. qui cõtra. ſur la fin. C. de inceſt. nu.
notes.gloss: The same law is cited at annot-094 {c} and {g}, with Baldus and Salicetus on it.
